names.name: Alabama white sauce
names.said: A tub of it goes on the table in north Alabama the way a red sauce does everywhere else.

text.what: A mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce, thin, pale and sharp. Typical ingredients are vinegar, lemon juice, salt, pepper, cayenne pepper and horseradish stirred into mayonnaise. It goes on barbecue chicken, which is an Alabama speciality, and on wings — dunked whole rather than brushed.
text.story:
White sauce was invented in Decatur, Alabama in 1925. It is believed to have been made by Bob Gibson at Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q there.

Alabama barbecue centres on pork cooked in open pits over hickory, with oak and pecan also used. A vinegar-based sauce like North Carolina's is common in the north of the state; a tomato-based one is usual south of Birmingham. White sauce stayed a north Alabama thing until 1994, when it began to be bottled and sold commercially.

Barbecue became popular in Alabama in the early 19th century, with roots in Native American cooking. Local militias held barbecues to get members to turn up for yearly drills, and they served as political and civic gatherings; by the late 1820s some social reformers opposed them, arguing they encouraged "political debasement" or that the alcohol and merrymaking were a moral problem. They failed. The first barbecue restaurants opened in the 1890s; the oldest continuously operating one in the state is Golden Rule Bar-B-Q, founded in 1891. In 2015 the Alabama Department of Tourism ran "The Year of Alabama Barbecue".
text.how: Dunk, do not brush. A whole smoked or fried chicken goes into the tub and comes out coated; wings go in by the basket. Mayonnaise splits over direct heat, so the sauce meets the bird after the fire, not during. It doubles as a dressing for the slaw beside it.
text.today: Bottled since 1994 and now sold nationally by several Alabama makers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Saw's Alabama White Sauce reads 300 mg sodium, 1 g sugar and 17 g fat in a 2-tablespoon serving — 150 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon, with soybean oil first and two vinegars on the list. Big Bob Gibson's own bottle returns no record in FoodData Central, so its panel is not on this disk. Nobody publishes a Scoville number.

profile.note: Saw's Alabama White Sauce, 12 fl oz. Label serving is 2 Tbsp (28 g); sodium 300 mg and sugars 1 g per serving, so 150 mg and 0.5 g per tablespoon. This is a Birmingham bottle, not Decatur's: Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q, which the invention is credited to, returns no record in FoodData Central, so its panel is not on this disk. pepper_rank is 0 because no chile is named on the label — only 'spices' at 7 and paprika at 14, and the cayenne and horseradish that descriptions of the sauce name do not appear on this one. The brand owner name is as the USDA record carries it. No Scoville number is published.

recipes.title: Barbecued squirrels
recipes.author: Marion Harland
ingredients: a teaspoonful, each, of sugar and made mustard
a half teaspoonful, each, of salt and pepper
recipes.text: Broil, as already directed, lay upon a hot dish, ribs downward, and cover with a sauce made by heating together four tablespoonfuls of vinegar with two of butter; a teaspoonful, each, of sugar and made mustard, a half teaspoonful, each, of salt and pepper. Boil one minute; pour over the squirrels, and let them stand, covered, ten minutes before serving.
recipes.note: Copied verbatim, old spellings kept. Not white sauce — no mayonnaise, and squirrels rather than chicken — but the same manoeuvre: a sharp fat-and-vinegar sauce poured over meat after the fire, and left to sit ten minutes.
